exam-15-q01.why_correct_en: The Middle Ages saw the development of a national culture and identity. After the Norman Conquest, the king and his noblemen had spoken Norman French and the peasants had continued to speak Anglo-Saxon.

exam-15-q02.why_correct_en: After the Seven Years' War ended in 1763, Britain faced heavy debt and the cost of keeping troops in North America. Parliament argued that the colonies should contribute to their defence and passed the Stamp Act in 1765, directly taxing newspapers, legal documents and other printed material. The central dispute was not simply the amount of tax but who had authority to impose it. The colonies elected no members to the Westminster Parliament and argued that only their own elected colonial assemblies could consent to taxation: 'No taxation without representation.' Britain replied that Parliament virtually represented all imperial subjects. Although the Stamp Act was repealed in 1766, the Declaratory Act asserted Parliament's authority to legislate for the colonies in all cases. Later duties, the Tea Act and coercive measures prolonged the conflict. The Boston Tea Party in 1773 was followed by punitive legislation, and fighting began at Lexington and Concord in 1775. On 4 July 1776, the 13 colonies adopted the Declaration of Independence. It listed taxation without consent among many grievances and argued that legitimate government derives its powers from the consent of the governed. Tax was therefore a trigger for a wider struggle over representation, legislative authority and self-government.

exam-15-q03.why_correct_en: This happened in 1649. Charles I believed strongly in divinely authorised monarchy and clashed with Parliament over taxation, law and religion. He governed without Parliament from 1629 to 1640; after war expenses forced him to summon it again, the conflict eventually produced the English Civil War in 1642. Parliament's New Model Army defeated the Royalists and captured the king. Charles continued secret negotiations and sought Scottish military support, helping trigger the Second Civil War in 1648. Army leaders concluded that he could not be trusted. After the Army purged MPs opposed to a trial, the Rump Parliament created a High Court of Justice. Charles was accused of waging war against his own people as a tyrant and traitor. His public trial opened in Westminster Hall on 20 January 1649. He refused to recognise the court's authority but was convicted and beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall on 30 January. The monarchy and House of Lords were abolished, and on 19 May England was declared a Commonwealth and Free State. Oliver Cromwell became Lord Protector in 1653; after his death the regime destabilised, and Charles II restored the monarchy in 1660. Strictly speaking, the United Kingdom did not yet exist: England was the state first declared a republic.

exam-15-q04.why_correct_en: Some of the most commercially successful films of all time, including the two highest-grossing film franchises (Harry Potter and James Bond), have been produced in the UK.

exam-15-q05.why_correct_en: Farming reached Britain about 6,000 years ago, around 4000 BC, largely through migrants from continental Europe. They did not make a single direct journey from south-eastern Europe to Britain. Their nearer route probably came through France, while their deeper ancestry traced back to early farmers around the Aegean and Anatolia, in modern Turkey. These populations moved west mainly along the Mediterranean into Iberia, then followed the Atlantic coast through France before crossing the English Channel. A different stream of early farmers had moved through central Europe along the Danube, but ancient DNA shows that Britain's Neolithic farmers were genetically closer to Iberian and Mediterranean groups. A 2019 study compared genomes from six Mesolithic and 67 Neolithic individuals in Britain. The major ancestry change around 4000 BC supports farming being introduced mainly by incoming continental farmers rather than simply adopted by local hunter-gatherers, although the newcomers carried small amounts of hunter-gatherer ancestry. Cereals, livestock, pottery, tools and new burial traditions appeared with the Neolithic culture.

exam-15-q06.why_correct_en: The time was fixed by the Armistice rather than being a natural or accidental endpoint. After overnight negotiations, German and Allied representatives signed the Armistice at about 5.00 am on 11 November 1918 in Ferdinand Foch's railway carriage in the Forest of Compiegne, France. Its first clause required operations on land and in the air to cease six hours after signature, so the ceasefire on the Western Front took effect at 11.00 am. The interval allowed orders to be transmitted along the front, although fighting continued and soldiers died during those final hours. The 'eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month' subsequently became the symbol of Armistice Day and remembrance. Strictly, the Armistice stopped the fighting; the Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919.

exam-15-q07.why_correct_en: True. Court orders can be obtained to protect a person from being forced into a marriage, or to protect a person in a forced marriage.

exam-15-q08.why_correct_en: Mary Peters won the women's athletics pentathlon at the 1972 Munich Olympics. This was not modern pentathlon: the women's athletics event comprised the 100 metres hurdles, shot put, high jump, long jump and 200 metres. Peters took the lead after the second event and finished with 4,801 points, then a world record, only ten points ahead of West Germany's Heide Rosendahl. Because the final scores still had to be calculated after the 200 metres, Peters first realised she had won when Rosendahl embraced her. Peters was 33 and competing at her third Olympic Games.

exam-15-q09.why_correct_en: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, if an accused person is aged 10 to 17, the case is normally heard in a Youth Court in front of up to three specially trained magistrates or a District Judge.

exam-15-q10.why_correct_en: A Turing machine is a theoretical mathematical device invented by Alan Turing (1912-54), a British mathematician, in the 1930s.

exam-15-q11.why_correct_en: Domesday Book is not a book about the end of the world. Domesday is an older form of Doomsday, while Old English doom meant law or judgement. The name became attached to the record after the survey. Medieval writers compared its authority with the Christian Last Judgement: everyone was called to account and there was no appeal from the final decision. William I's survey similarly recorded land, holders, value, resources and tax obligations in exceptional detail, and royal administrators treated it as authoritative evidence in disputes. William ordered the survey at Christmas 1085 and it was conducted in 1086. It was also known as the Book of Winchester because it was initially kept in the royal treasury there. The familiar Chinese title is therefore best understood as a land register whose judgement was treated as final, not as a prophecy of doomsday.

exam-15-q12.why_correct_en: Scientists led by Ernest Rutherford, working at Manchester and then Cambridge University, were the first to ‘split the atom‘ and took part in the Manhattan Project in the United States, which developed the atomic bomb.

exam-15-q13.why_correct_en: Auld Lang Syne is written mainly in Scots, not Scottish Gaelic. Scots is a Germanic language closely related to English, whereas Scottish Gaelic is a distinct Celtic language. Word by word, auld means old, lang means long, and syne means since or ago; the phrase evokes times long past and is commonly understood as 'for old times' sake'. Words such as twa, hae, braes and wee are characteristic Scots forms. Robert Burns collected an older Scottish folk song and adapted or extended its words, sending his version to the music publisher James Johnson in 1788. It later appeared in The Scots Musical Museum. The song is now sung at New Year, including Scotland's Hogmanay celebrations, to remember old friends and shared times.

exam-15-q14.why_correct_en: The Civil war between the king and Parliament began in 1642. The country split into those who supported the king (the Cavaliers) and those who supported Parliament (the Roundheads).

exam-15-q15.why_correct_en: Housesteads and Vindolanda are both in Northumberland in northern England, in the central sector of the Hadrian's Wall frontier between Newcastle and Carlisle, near Hexham and Bardon Mill. Hadrian's Wall itself runs about 73 miles from Wallsend in the east to Bowness-on-Solway in the west. Housesteads Roman Fort stands directly on the Wall near Haydon Bridge, roughly midway along it, on the Whin Sill escarpment. Vindolanda is near Bardon Mill, about one mile south of the curtain wall. It stands on the earlier Roman Stanegate road and its first forts pre-dated the construction of Hadrian's Wall, which began in AD 122; it later served as an important construction and garrison base for the Wall. The question therefore uses 'part of Hadrian's Wall' in the wider sense of the Roman frontier complex, not to mean that Vindolanda is built into the stone wall itself.

exam-15-q16.why_correct_en: Puritans were Christians within Protestant Christianity, not followers of a completely separate religion. Christianity is the broad category, Protestantism is one of its major traditions, and the Puritans were a reform movement within English Protestantism in the 16th and 17th centuries. All Puritans were Protestants, but not all Protestants were Puritans. Protestant describes Christians whose churches emerged from the Reformation and rejected the Pope's supreme authority over their churches, although Protestant denominations differ greatly. The name Puritan reflects their wish to 'purify' the Church of England further. They believed the English Reformation had retained too many Catholic ceremonies, vestments, set prayers and episcopal structures. Many sought reform from within the Church of England; others became Separatists or Nonconformists. Often influenced by Reformed or Calvinist theology, they emphasised the Bible, preaching, moral discipline, Sabbath observance and plain worship.

exam-15-q17.why_correct_en: The name Fenian comes from the Fianna of Irish mythology, not from the surname of a nineteenth-century politician. The Fianna were a legendary warrior band led by Fionn mac Cumhaill, anglicised as Finn MacCool, and portrayed as defenders of Ireland. In 1858 James Stephens founded the secret revolutionary Irish Republican Brotherhood in Dublin. That year the Irish nationalist and Gaelic scholar John O'Mahony established its American sister organisation, the Fenian Brotherhood, in New York. He took the name from the Fianna to present its members as modern warriors for Irish independence. Both organisations sought an independent Irish republic through revolution, and their members and wider movement became known as Fenians. From the 1860s Fenianism became a general term for revolutionary Irish nationalism. It is distinct from the Fianna Fail political party founded in 1926; in some modern contexts Fenian is also used as a sectarian slur against Irish people or Catholics.

exam-15-q18.why_correct_en: The decade of the 1960s was a period of significant social change. It was known as the ‘swinging sixties’. There was growth in British fashion, cinema and popular music. Two well-known pop music groups at the time were The Beatles and The Rolling Stones.

exam-15-q19.why_correct_en: In the UK, you must be at least 17 years to drive a car or motorcycle and you must have a driving licence to drive on public roads.

exam-15-q20.why_correct_en: False. Members of the House of Lords are not elected by the public. As of 2026, the House mainly comprises life peers and 26 Church of England bishop seats. Political parties can propose political nominees. People may nominate themselves or others for non-party-political Crossbench membership, and the independent House of Lords Appointments Commission assesses those candidates and vets every life-peer nomination for propriety. The Prime Minister formally advises the King, who creates the life peerage by Letters Patent; a new member must then take the oath before sitting and voting. A life peerage lasts only for that person's life and does not pass a Lords seat to their children. The Lords Spiritual comprise the Archbishops of Canterbury and York, the Bishops of London, Durham and Winchester, and other senior Church of England bishops; their seats pass on when they leave episcopal office. Following the House of Lords (Hereditary Peers) Act 2026, the remaining hereditary peers ceased on 29 April 2026 to sit merely by virtue of hereditary peerages.

exam-15-q21.why_correct_en: In 1833 the Emancipation Act abolished slavery throughout the British Empire.

exam-15-q22.why_correct_en: The Home Secretary is responsible for crime, policing and immigration.
